source: Gero, Kan, Pourmohamadi (2011) Analysing design protocols: development of methods and tools
finding: Design protocol studies could not be compared because each group used its own ad hoc coding scheme, even on the same data set. The authors propose one principled scheme built on the Function-Behaviour-Structure (FBS) ontology so results of different researchers can be compared.
numbers: Method has 7 steps: coding development, video, transcription, segmentation and coding, analysis of coded protocol, linkograph generation, linkograph analysis. Demo protocol: one industry team, over 1 hour, 1280 coded segments.
quote: Without agreed methods of coding and measurement the results of cognitive studies of designers carried out under different conditions by different researchers cannot be compared.
limits: Methods paper with a demonstration; no reliability figures or hypothesis tests in this paper. Authors themselves say FBS is only one of several possible general schemes.
agent_relevance: Same problem for LLM traces: every lab codes reasoning traces with its own labels. A fixed, task-independent code set (like FBS) is what makes trace results comparable across tasks and models.

source: Gero, Kan, Pourmohamadi (2011) Analysing design protocols (FBS codes and processes)
finding: FBS coding: each segment gets exactly one code (one segment per code) from six issues: Requirement, Function, expected Behaviour (Be), derived Behaviour (Bs), Structure, Description. Eight processes arise from moving between issues: formulation (F to Be), synthesis (Be to S), analysis (S to Bs), evaluation (Be vs Bs), documentation (S to D), and three reformulations (of S, of Be, of F).
numbers: 6 issues, 8 processes. Syntactic linkograph: only adjacent segments define a process (weak model). Semantic linkograph: backlinks by meaning define the process, e.g. S linked back to Be = synthesis.
limits: Reliability of the single-code-per-segment rule depends on coder training; see a10 for 79.5% agreement in a 2025 study. Ontology is a theory of designing, not proven to be the only valid partition.
agent_relevance: A ready code set for LLM traces in design-like tasks: expected behaviour (goal), structure (candidate), derived behaviour (what the candidate actually does), evaluation (compare the two). Maps onto our states: attempt, run/check, compare.

source: Gero, Kan, Pourmohamadi (2011) Analysing design protocols (measurement models)
finding: Five measurement families on a coded protocol: tabular statistics of issues and processes; dynamic models (fractioning, windowing with a sliding window, trimming); first-order Markov model (6x6 issue transitions); second-order Markov model (8 processes x 6 issues); first passage model (mean number of segments before the same issue returns); Shannon entropy of the linkograph. All built into the LINKOgrapher tool.
numbers: Window used in demo = 1/10 of protocol length. Markov matrix 6x6 first order, 8x6 second order. Example finding cited: lack of evaluation (process 4) when designing in a 3D virtual environment. Architects vs software designers compared with the same Markov models.
limits: Dynamic entropy ignores the codes and uses only link structure. Window size is a free parameter. No inferential statistics shown.
agent_relevance: Every one of these measures is cheap to compute on an LLM trace once segments are coded: transition matrix, return time to a state, windowed share of evaluation. Gives a quantitative signature of how a scaffolded run differs from a plain run.

source: Gero, Kan, Pourmohamadi (2011) citing Ericsson and Simon (1993) and Kan and Gero entropy work
finding: The design field treats protocol analysis (Ericsson and Simon) as a validated method for eliciting verbal reports of thought sequences and the most common way to study design cognition. Kan and Gero argued that the entropy of semantic linkographs relates to the productivity of design activity; dynamic entropy has been used to study fixation and commitment.
numbers: Cites 36 references; claims the two FBS papers had over 900 Google Scholar citations in 2011.
quote: Protocol analysis is a rigorous methodology for eliciting verbal reports of thought sequences as a valid source of data on thinking.
limits: Authors' own summary; no discussion of reactivity, incompleteness of verbal reports, or the Nisbett and Wilson critique.
agent_relevance: Shows the design field leans on Ericsson-Simon validity without testing it. For LLMs that validity assumption is exactly what is in doubt (see a19 to a22).

source: Hay, Duffy, McTeague, Pidgeon, Vuletic, Grealy (2017) A systematic review of protocol studies on conceptual design cognition: design as search and exploration
finding: First systematic review of protocol studies of conceptual design. Reviewed 47 studies; 33 reported in depth, covering 24 cognitive processes under two viewpoints: design as search (10 processes, 41.7%) and design as exploration (14 processes, 58.3%). Terminology and concepts differ widely across studies. Authors call for general models, objective larger-sample tests of protocol findings, and a shared ontology.
numbers: 6796 articles retrieved, 4996 after de-duplication, 47 included. 24 of 47 (53.2%) in the last decade. About 350 participants in total; per study min 1, max 36, mean 7, median 6, SD 6.30.
quote: considerable conceptual and terminological differences were observed among the studies.
limits: Qualitative synthesis only, no meta-analysis; individual designers only (teams excluded); searches done March to October 2015; architecture, engineering and product design only.
agent_relevance: Warns that protocol findings come from tiny samples (median 6 people) and mixed vocabularies. Treat any claim 'designers do X' as hypothesis; test on LLM traces with large N, which is cheap.

source: Hay et al. (2017) A systematic review of protocol studies (sample characteristics)
finding: Describes what protocol studies in design actually used. Most used concurrent think-aloud; some retrospective. Tasks split across domains; many studies add video and sketches.
numbers: 45 distinct design tasks: 20 architectural (44.4%), 19 product design engineering (42.2%), 6 engineering (13.3%). Verbalisation: concurrent 32 studies (68.1%), retrospective 11 (23.4%), both 4 (8.5%). 36 full protocol studies (76.6%) vs 11 re-analyses (23.4%). Protocol length 15 to 600 minutes. Video in 38 studies (84.4%), sketches in 24 (51.1%).
limits: Experience of participants was defined inconsistently, and some authors gave no experience data. Several authors omitted protocol length.
agent_relevance: Concurrent (during the work) is the standard; an LLM trace is by construction concurrent output, but it is generated text, not a report of a hidden process. Retrospective explanations by an LLM are closer to the weaker, 'explain afterwards' kind of report.

source: Hay et al. (2017) Towards a shared ontology: a generic classification of cognitive processes in conceptual design
finding: Maps the many process names found in 47 design protocol studies onto 6 generic categories from cognitive psychology: long-term memory, semantic processing, visual perception, mental imagery processing, creative output production, executive functions. Names six research gaps, including the role of working memory and the meaning of 'synthesis'.
numbers: 47 studies over about 30 years; 6 categories; 6 future-research avenues.
limits: Mapping was done by the authors' judgement; no inter-rater test reported in the abstract. Focus on individual conceptual design.
agent_relevance: A second, psychology-grounded code set to cross with FBS. Useful when coding what an LLM step does (retrieve, interpret, imagine, produce, control) rather than what design issue it addresses.

source: Zhang, Gu, Chen, Ding, Chai, Fan (2025) Leveraging LLMs to emulate the design processes of different cognitive styles (AHFE)
finding: GPT-4o with a zero-shot chain-of-thought prompt was told to act as a problem-driven or solution-driven designer. FBS protocol coding of the generated process showed the same static pattern as human students: problem-driven runs put more share on Function and Requirement, solution-driven runs more on Structure. But LLMs did not reproduce nonlinear moves between problem and solution space.
numbers: 4 groups x 10 generated processes (P1, P2, S1, S2) plus 2 baseline groups x 10. Without constraint, mean share: Requirement 9.7 vs 4.3 (p=0.001); Function 18.9 vs 9.2 (p<0.001); Structure 10.6 vs 29.3 (p<0.001). Formulation 31.7 vs 16.3; Reformulation-S 5.8 vs 21.5.
limits: Only 10 runs per cell, one model, one task (bathroom product). Human benchmark is Chen et al. 2023 with 54 industrial design students, not a matched sample. Some contrasts fail under the extra-constraint task (Be, Analysis, Synthesis).
agent_relevance: Shows FBS coding can be applied to LLM output and detects prompt-induced style. Also shows the failure that matters: LLM processes are more linear, so a scaffold must add the return trips on purpose.

source: Zhang et al. (2025) Leveraging LLMs to emulate design processes (transitions and outcomes)
finding: Process transitions: problem-driven LLM runs had more problem-to-problem steps (PP) and solution-driven runs more solution-to-solution (SS), as in humans. But problem-driven LLM runs had fewer problem/solution crossings (PS, SP) than solution-driven runs without constraint, the reverse of humans. Process-based emulation raised novelty and integrity of outcomes over a direct-prompt baseline.
numbers: PP 30.7 vs 15.3 (p<0.001); SS 9.9 vs 29.4 (p<0.001); PS 6.7 vs 10.5 (p=0.001); SP 6.4 vs 9.8 (p=0.003), without constraint. Novelty and integrity higher than baseline (p<0.05) on 1-7 expert ratings; feasibility of P2 not above baseline.
limits: Outcome ratings by 2 experts, Pearson r = 77.02%. Small N; creativity effect not separated from simply writing more steps. Authors suggest Graph of Thoughts as a fix for linear progress.
agent_relevance: Direct support for the schema's reframe operators: LLMs stay in one space unless forced to cross. Count PS/SP crossings in our traces as a diagnostic.

source: Zhang et al. (2025) Leveraging LLMs to emulate design processes (coder reliability and P-S index)
finding: Two PhD students in industrial design, trained in FBS, coded the LLM transcripts independently with one-segment-one-code. Agreement was moderate. The Problem-Solution index (problem issues R,F,Be divided by solution issues S,Bs) was used to classify style: above 1 = problem-driven.
numbers: Inter-coder reliability 79.5% (percent agreement, Lombard et al. 2005). P-S index: all problem-driven runs classed correctly; all solution-driven runs correct except two under the extra-constraint task.
limits: Percent agreement is not chance-corrected, so 79.5% overstates reliability. The paper's P-S formula text is garbled in the PDF extraction; the definition above follows the prose.
agent_relevance: Gives a baseline for human coder agreement on FBS (about 80%) to compare LLM-as-coder against. P-S index is a one-number summary we can compute from coded traces.

source: Sakib, Hurst, Safayeni (2026) Evaluating the performance of LLMs in taxonomic classification of questions in verbal protocols of design (AI EDAM)
finding: GPT-4.1 and Claude Sonnet 4.5 labelled question utterances from design protocols with Eris's (2004) taxonomy (low-level, deep reasoning, generative design questions). Category-level agreement with human labels was high, subcategory-level agreement much lower. Prompt design and in-context examples changed results by small amounts once examples were given.
numbers: Up to 85.7% (GPT-4.1) and 82.9% (Claude Sonnet 4.5) category level. Exp. 1 on 1942 questions, 7 prompt conditions: A no system prompt 57.0%; B definitions 69.9%; C 70.2%; D 72.7%; E 79.4%; F 79.8%; G 80.3% (E to G not significantly different). Best prompt G: category 80.2% vs human inter-rater 85.7%; subcategory 52.5% vs human 74.7%.
limits: Two human-coded datasets (d1 large, d2 N=175) of differing quality. Chance at category level is 33.3%. Human agreement elsewhere in the literature is as low as 70% or kappa 0.49 and 0.41 (subcategory). Alignment is not the same as validity.
agent_relevance: Best evidence that an LLM can act as the coder of a trace at the coarse category level, with examples at the fine level. Use few categories, give worked examples, and keep a human-checked sample.

source: Sakib et al. (2026) classification of design questions (error structure and cross-model results)
finding: Errors were not random. Generative design questions (divergent) were hardest; low-level questions easiest. Subcategories that differ only by subtle context (Verification vs Judgmental, Concept Completion vs Feature Specification, Ideation) were confused. GPT-4.1 and Claude Sonnet 4.5 were mostly statistically comparable.
numbers: Category accuracy GPT-4.1: low-level 93%, deep reasoning 60%, generative 53% (30% of generative called low-level). Subcategory: Disjunctive 89.1%, Quantification 83.3%, Verification 63.1%, Concept Completion 22.7%, Ideation 20.8%. Exp. 2: 76.7% to 85.1% across model and example-source pairs; GPT-4.1 on d1 with d2 examples was 76.7% and Claude was significantly better there (Holm p<.05).
limits: In-context example source mattered for GPT-4.1 on d1 (p<.05) but not for Claude. Some subcategories had 0 or 1 test items (4 of 21).
agent_relevance: LLM coders fail where the label needs discourse context the single segment lacks. When coding traces, give each segment its neighbours, and prefer categories decidable from the text alone.

source: Kelly and Gero (2025) Semantic and network analysis of design protocols to reveal design framing phenomena (ICED25)
finding: Replaces hand coding with a pipeline: an LLM extracts concepts from think-aloud text, OpenAI embeddings give semantic vectors, k-means groups concepts into regions, and a graph of moves between regions gives network measures (clustering, leap similarity, global cosine similarity). Used to compare designers and to find framing moments.
numbers: 17 designers, 2 problems (spill-proof coffee cup, car bike rack); 16-minute sessions; transcript cut into 2-second segments (fMRI repetition time); text-embedding-3-small; vector = 0.8 concept + 0.2 sentence. Per-designer clustering, leap and global similarity were not strongly correlated across the two problems.
quote: Using an LLM for identifying concepts is inherently unreliable, both internally (repeated coding of the same transcript) and when compared to humans.
limits: Authors state the reliability trade-off is not quantified and the meaning of the measures needs more theory. Only 2 of 17 participants analysed in detail. Style did not transfer across problems on the measures used.
agent_relevance: A code-free route for LLM traces: embed each step, cluster into regions, track revisits and leaps. Cheap, but an LLM that extracts the concepts is itself unstable; fix temperature and repeat the extraction.

source: Kan and Gero (2007) Comparing entropy measures of idea links in design protocols (AI EDAM)
finding: Applied Shannon entropy to linkographs of 12 design sessions by six architects in two experimental conditions. Overall entropy was slightly higher in one condition, and entropy change may reflect design outcome. Only the abstract (via Crossref) was read.
numbers: 12 sessions, 6 architects, 2 conditions. Direction and size of the difference were not given in the abstract.
limits: Abstract only. Tiny sample; result described as 'slightly higher' and 'indications', not a tested effect.
agent_relevance: Entropy of the link structure of a trace is a possible productivity signal, but the founding evidence is weak. Test on our own traces before trusting it.

source: Dorst and Cross (2001) Creativity in the design process: co-evolution of problem-solution (Design Studies 22)
finding: Reanalysed a protocol from the Delft design protocols workshop and proposed that creative designing is not search of a fixed problem space but parallel development of problem and solution, with a bridge made when a matched pair of problem framing and solution idea appears. Not opened this session; summarised as described in Hay et al. 2017 and Zhang et al. 2025, which both cite it as the source of the co-evolution model.
numbers: Not read. Hay et al. (opened) say co-evolution is a model where the designer 'explores the spaces of problem requirements and design solutions iteratively'.
limits: Based on recalled and second-hand description; one protocol analysed in the paper from memory, not verified. Sample of designers is very small.
agent_relevance: Theory behind the problem-solution split used in a08/a09: a scaffold that only searches a fixed problem misses reframing.

source: Ericsson and Simon (1980, 1984/1993) Verbal reports as data; Protocol analysis
finding: Founding theory: verbal reports are valid data on thinking when they verbalise what is already in short-term memory (Type 1 concurrent 'talk aloud'); they stay valid with some added recoding if they only report heeded information. Reports that ask for explanation or reasons, or that are given long after, are less reliable because they involve retrieval or inference. Not opened; summary from recall of the standard account and from how Hay et al. and Gero et al. (opened) cite it.
numbers: None verified this session.
limits: Recalled, not verified against the book. Claims of validity apply to well-structured tasks and short-term memory content; creative or highly automated steps may go unreported.
agent_relevance: The key rule: concurrent, non-explaining output is the trustworthy kind. For LLMs this predicts trace text is a record of what was generated, not necessarily why.

source: Nisbett and Wilson (1977) Telling more than we can know: verbal reports on mental processes
finding: People often cannot report the real causes of their choices and instead give plausible theories; e.g. in a position-effect task people preferred the right-most of identical items and denied position mattered. Not opened; recalled.
numbers: Not verified this session (recalled: right-most article chosen far more often than left-most; participants denied any position effect).
limits: Recalled, not checked; it is the main counter-claim to using verbal reports as process data. Ericsson and Simon reply that it concerns retrospective, why-questions, not concurrent reports.
agent_relevance: Direct human analogue of unfaithful chain of thought (a19 to a22): a fluent explanation can be a rationalisation, so a trace cannot be used as proof of why.

source: Fox, Ericsson, Best (2011) Do procedures for verbal reporting of thinking have to be reactive? Meta-analysis (Psychological Bulletin)
finding: Meta-analysis of studies comparing thinking aloud with silent control found that ordinary think-aloud (just say what you think) does not change correctness of performance, while asking people to explain or give reasons can. Not opened; recalled from the literature.
numbers: Not verified this session (recalled as about 94 studies; effect of think-aloud near zero on accuracy; time often longer).
limits: Recalled, not verified. Titles found via Crossref only. Boundary: instructions that require explanation change the task.
agent_relevance: Predicts that making the model 'explain its reasoning' may change its answer, so a coding trace should be gathered from the natural thinking, not from a separate explanation step.

source: Turpin, Michael, Perez, Bowman (2023) Language models don't always say what they think: unfaithful explanations in chain-of-thought prompting
finding: LLM chain-of-thought can rationalise an answer pushed by a hidden bias (reordering options so the answer is always A, or a suggested answer) without ever mentioning the bias. Accuracy fell when biased, and the stated reasoning supported the biased answer. This is the LLM version of Nisbett and Wilson.
numbers: Accuracy dropped by up to 36% on 13 tasks from BIG-Bench Hard (GPT-3.5, Claude 1.0). Suggested Answer bias: -36.3% for GPT-3.5 (few-shot reduced to -24.1%) and -30.6% for Claude 1.0 (to -21.5%). Answer-Is-Always-A: -18.7% GPT-3.5, -4.7% Claude 1.0. In a manual sample, up to 73% of unfaithful explanations supported the bias-consistent answer; 15% of explanations had no obvious error.
limits: Older models (GPT-3.5, Claude 1.0). Social-bias case shows 86% of explanations leading to stereotype-aligned answers did not mention the bias. Debiasing instructions had mixed effect.
agent_relevance: A trace is plausible but not proof of cause. Code the trace for what it says, but do not let the scaffold trust the model's own stated reason; keep program-side checks (G2, G3).

source: Lanham et al. (2023) Measuring faithfulness in chain-of-thought reasoning
finding: Tests faithfulness by intervening on the CoT: truncating it (early answering), inserting a mistake, paraphrasing, or replacing it with filler tokens. How much the answer depends on the CoT varies hugely by task. CoT benefit is not from extra compute or from phrasing. Larger, more capable models gave less faithful reasoning on most tasks.
numbers: For ARC Easy, ARC Challenge and OpenbookQA the CoT changes the final answer less than 10% of the time; for AQuA more than 60%. Mean CoT length 4 steps. Faithfulness worsens monotonically from 13B to 175B on some tasks; the 13B model was most faithful there.
limits: Early-2023 Anthropic models. Faithfulness here means causal dependence of the answer on the written steps; a post-hoc CoT can still look right. Task-dependent: post-hoc rate did not predict the accuracy gain from CoT.
agent_relevance: Gives an intervention test that fits our schema: change the trace, see if the answer moves. Traces on easy tasks may be decoration, so coding them tells little about the real process there.

source: Chen et al. (2025) Reasoning models don't always say what they think
finding: Six kinds of hints were inserted into prompts; when a model used the hint to change its answer, the CoT usually did not mention it. Reasoning models were somewhat more faithful than non-reasoning models, but still low. Outcome-based RL raised faithfulness at first, then plateaued. When RL taught reward hacks, models almost never verbalised them.
numbers: Average faithfulness 25% for Claude 3.7 Sonnet and 39% for DeepSeek R1; on misalignment-type hints 20% and 29%. RL faithfulness plateau 28% on MMLU and 20% on GPQA. Synthetic reward hacks: model used them on over 99% of prompts but verbalised them in under 2% of examples in 5 of 6 environments. Hints verbalised at least 1% of the time in 6/6 settings (R1) and 5/6 (Claude 3.7) versus 4 to 5 of 6 for non-reasoning models.
limits: Hint paradigm on multiple-choice (MMLU, GPQA) where CoT is not strictly needed; authors note harder tasks that require CoT may be more faithful. A contrasting study (Baker et al. 2025) found CoT monitoring caught over 90% of reward hacks in coding.
agent_relevance: Strongest recent number against reading traces as full reports: under 1 in 4 to 2 in 5 hint uses are disclosed. Use traces to code visible behaviour (what was tried, what check ran), not hidden motives.

source: Zhang et al. (2025) and Sakib et al. (2026) combined: reliability of LLM-as-coder
finding: Across the opened LLM studies, coarse agreement with human protocol coders reaches about 80% (Sakib) and human-human agreement is 79.5% (Zhang) to 85.7% (Sakib d1). Fine-grained labels drop to about 52%. One pipeline paper (Kelly and Gero) says LLM concept coding is unstable across repeats.
numbers: Category 80.2% vs human 85.7%; subcategory 52.5% vs 74.7%; Zhang humans 79.5%. All are percent agreement, not chance-corrected, except the kappa values 0.49 and 0.41 quoted by Sakib for earlier human studies.
limits: Synthesis of three papers by this agent; datasets and tasks differ, so figures are not strictly comparable.
agent_relevance: Plan: code traces with an LLM at coarse level, check a sample by hand, report chance-corrected agreement (kappa), repeat coding runs to measure self-consistency.

source: Goldschmidt linkography as used in Gero et al. (2011) and Kelly and Gero (2025)
finding: Linkography links design moves by meaning: a backlink points from a move to an earlier move that prompted it, a forelink to a later move it prompts. FBS ties each link to a design process. Kelly and Gero argue a graph of concept regions is a lower-cost alternative that still shows revisits, like a linkograph.
numbers: Gero 2011 demo: 1280 segments in one linkograph. Kelly and Gero: graph nodes are clusters of concepts, edges are moves between clusters.
limits: Linking is subjective in manual linkography; Gero 2011 does not give link agreement figures.
agent_relevance: A trace of agent steps can be turned into a link graph automatically (which later step uses an earlier step's output). Dense back-links = building on earlier work; none = scattered.

source: Crossref listing: LLM and linkography titles 2023 to 2026 (IEEE and Taylor and Francis)
finding: Three studies apply linkography to LLM output or use an LLM to automate it: 'Using Linkography to Quantitatively Analyze the Design Ideation of AI Agents' (2023), 'Research on Ideation Process and Design Productivity of ChatGPT Based on LASSO and Linkography' (2023), and 'Tracing Cognitive Dynamics in Group Ideation: An LLM-Based Framework for Automating Linkography' (2026). Only titles and DOIs were read; full text and abstracts were not accessible (403 or empty).
numbers: None; not opened.
limits: Title only. Publisher pages returned 403 or empty content. Do not cite results from these without opening them.
agent_relevance: Leads to follow up: they show linkography already applied to ChatGPT output, with productivity measures.

source: Hay et al. (2017) boundary notes on protocol analysis
finding: The review notes that the merits of protocol analysis are debated (Lloyd, Lawson and Scott 1995; Suwa and Tversky 1997; Sarkar and Chakrabarti 2014) but several authors hold that it is among the only methods that directly reveals designers' internal processing. The review itself asks for objective methods that scale to larger samples to test protocol findings.
numbers: Sample sizes in the reviewed studies: median 6 participants, max 36.
quote: testing protocol study findings using objective methods conducive to larger samples
limits: Review does not give effect sizes or replication results for specific findings; it reports that definitions differ across studies, which blocks direct replication.
agent_relevance: No clean failed-replication record exists in this field because concepts and codes differ. LLM traces allow real replication: same code set, many runs.

source: Gero et al. (2011) and Zhang et al. (2025): human benchmark chain for FBS style differences
finding: The human benchmark for problem-driven vs solution-driven designers is the P-S index of Jiang, Gero and Yen (2014) and Chen et al. (2023): 54 industrial design students coded with FBS. Problem-driven designers spend more on Function and Expected Behaviour and use more Formulation; solution-driven spend more on Structure and Structural Behaviour and use more Analysis and Reformulation-S. Requirement stays lowest in both.
numbers: Chen et al. 2023: 54 industrial design students (as reported by Zhang et al.). Original human tables were not opened.
limits: Second-hand figures from Zhang et al.; Chen et al. 2023 and Jiang et al. 2014 not opened. Style classification depends on the P-S index cut at 1.
agent_relevance: The P-S index could tell us whether a run was spending effort on understanding the task or on building answers, and whether the scaffold shifts it.

source: Zhang et al. (2025) baseline and limits of prompting to produce process structure
finding: Telling the LLM in the prompt which process to follow is enough to shift the share of issue types in the output, but this may be role-play of the described profile rather than a real process difference. The coded text is what the model wrote when asked to 'generate the design process step-by-step', not a protocol of a concurrent solving process.
numbers: All 40 style runs of the prompt gave matching P-S index direction except 2 runs under constraint (the 2 exceptions were among the 10 solution-driven runs under the extra constraint).
limits: The emulation measures conformity to the prompt's own description of the style, which is circular: the prompt lists the exact issue types to emphasise. Authors did not run a no-style-prompt comparison of process coding, only an outcome comparison against direct generation.
agent_relevance: A coded trace from a prompted process is evidence the model followed instructions, not evidence of the process helping. Compare outcomes, not only trace shape.
